posts.title: SGURR NA BANACHDICH – AN ‘EASY’ IF DREADED, BLACK CUILLIN HIKE
posts.description: Length: 7.5km return Ascent: 936m Time taken: 5.5hrs S tart: Glenbrittle Youth Hostel Difficulty : no scrambling at all , no exposure , wide but very rocky and steep slopes. Rating: 5 stars The Gaelic poet Sorley MacLean described the Cuillin ridge as a symbol of ‘man’s heroic spirit rising above the tawdry. ’I can’t honestly say I approached this mountain with anything like a heroic spirit. More like ’a wee feartie approaches an intimidating Black Cuillin peak with trepidation.’ I’ve never been great withe edges and ledges and this has got worse with age.Now at 68 years old, my vertigo has been further honed by a growing timidity over very steep ground too.Hence, opting to hike Sgurr na Banachdich had me losing sleep and fighting off the terrible anxiety that can descend on me when I am worried about a hill.Happy holidays! posts.title: MUST VISIT VILLAGES IN THE LUBERON
posts.description: Gordes The priority for our last full day in the Luberon was the beautiful village of Gordes, another of France’s prettiest. So many of these! Yet for us , in modern parlance, exploring them ‘never grows old.’ The best view of Gordes’ honey stone buildings tumbling down the hillside is from the approach road from Roussillon.There is free parking at a large pull in which allows a wander to several viewpoints from the top of the cliffs.If only today’s town planing and building could achieve such pleasing results! We left the car in one of the car parks just outside the village and walked 5 mins or so up to the main square.This space was quite busy with traffic but it impressed given its domination by the walls of a 1,000 year old castle. posts.title: LAVENDER FIELDS AND THE ANCIENT VILLAGES OF THE LUBERON
posts.description: Many years ago we stayed near Lacoste in the Luberon, a beautiful, well-to-do area made famous by Peter Mayle in his book ‘A Year in Provence.’ It has glorious medieval stone villages, many of them perched and which look over well kept vineyards, wheat and lavender fields. This time we were staying for 3 nights in Roussillon, which we hadn’t yet visited and just under a 2 hour drive away. It’s known as an ochre village due to the houses being reddish/orange, given the adjacent ochre gorge from which their stone had been quarried. These various villages of the Vaucluse, as the department is called, had made an impression on us all those years ago – many are officially listed as France’s Most Beautiful Villages – so we were looking forward to a return visit. The motorway north was running well and not overly busy and we were soon taking the turn off we needed near Cavaillon.
